title: Sending Secrets Without Sharing a Secret First

sources.title: RFC 9180 — Hybrid Public Key Encryption
sources.notes: Introduces hybrid asymmetric/symmetric designs and KEM/KDF/AEAD composition. Episode distinguishes its conceptual wrapped-key teaching model from exact HPKE.

sources.title: RFC 5116 — An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
sources.notes: AEAD confidentiality/integrity interface, authentication failure, and scheme-specific nonce requirements.

sources.title: RFC 8446 — TLS 1.3
sources.notes: TLS1.3 uses authenticated key establishment and AEAD; static RSA key transport removed. Used to distinguish the simplified diagram from modern TLS.

sections.title: A secret on a public network
sections.narration: Alice sends Bob a message across an observable network. Eve can copy traffic. Sending a shared secret openly repeats the same problem, so we need complementary cryptographic capabilities.
sections.takeaway: A public network needs more than a promise that nobody is listening.

sections.title: Plaintext becomes ciphertext
sections.narration: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using a key. Decryption recovers it with the appropriate key. These changing letter tiles illustrate the idea; they are not a working cipher.
bullets: Illustrated symbols are not real crypto
sections.takeaway: Encryption conceals content through a keyed transformation.

sections.title: The algorithm can be public
sections.narration: A sound design does not rely on hiding its algorithm. Eve can know how encryption works and still lack the secret key. Public scrutiny helps uncover weaknesses.
bullets: Secrecy of design is not a foundation
sections.takeaway: Protect the key rather than relying on an unknown algorithm.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret
sections.narration: Symmetric encryption uses shared secret material for protection and recovery. Alice and Bob both need the correct key, while an observer may know the algorithm and see ciphertext.
sections.takeaway: A symmetric key must remain secret from unauthorized parties.

sections.title: A key is not simply a memorable password
sections.narration: Human passwords can be guessable. Cryptographic keys need suitable length and unpredictability; password systems require dedicated derivation mechanisms. Our tiny key symbols stand for properly generated material.
sections.takeaway: Use appropriate key generation rather than a memorable homemade key.

sections.title: The key-distribution problem
sections.narration: If Alice transmits the symmetric key openly, Eve can copy it and recover the protected message. The cipher has not failed; the required secret was exposed.
bullets: Sending K openly reveals the secret
sections.takeaway: Secure encryption still needs a sound way to establish or distribute keys.

sections.title: Give Bob a pair of keys
sections.narration: Bob’s public key can be distributed; his private key stays secret. In an appropriate encryption scheme, information protected for the public key is recovered using the private key.
sections.takeaway: A public/private key pair assigns different capabilities to each key.

sections.title: Publish the encryption key
sections.narration: Observers may obtain Bob’s public encryption key without gaining his private decryption capability. Alice must still authenticate whose key it is; publication alone does not establish identity.
bullets: Public also does not mean trusted
sections.takeaway: Public-key distribution and public-key authentication are different problems.

sections.title: Encrypt to Bob’s public key
sections.narration: Alice encrypts using Bob’s authenticated public key. Eve can observe the ciphertext and public key without obtaining Bob’s decryption capability, assuming the chosen scheme is sound.
bullets: Observing PK_B does not reveal SK_B
sections.takeaway: Use a suitable scheme and the intended recipient’s authenticated public key.

sections.title: Decrypt with the private key
sections.narration: Bob uses his private key to recover the protected information. The private key never belongs in the transmitted envelope. Compromise can expose data depending on the protocol’s properties.
bullets: The private key is not transmitted
sections.takeaway: Protecting private keys is part of protecting the communication.

sections.title: Why not encrypt every file this way?
sections.narration: Public-key operations have practical costs and constraints. Hybrid designs use their key-management advantages while symmetric encryption efficiently protects bulk data. The two techniques perform different jobs.
sections.takeaway: Hybrid designs combine complementary capabilities.

sections.title: Generate a fresh session key
sections.narration: Alice generates suitable random session key K. Fresh key material helps limit inappropriate reuse, but correct nonces, authentication, and key handling remain necessary throughout the protocol.
bullets: Generate fresh random session key K
sections.takeaway: A hybrid example begins with appropriate session key material.

sections.title: Protect the data with the session key
sections.narration: Authenticated symmetric encryption uses K to protect the data and produce verification information. The package includes ciphertext, a tag, and required nonce or metadata specified by the scheme.
sections.takeaway: Authenticated symmetric encryption protects the bulk message.

sections.title: Protect the session key for Bob
sections.narration: Our simplified key-transport model protects K using Bob’s authenticated public key. Modern hybrid standards may instead encapsulate and derive keys. The principle is not an exact TLS handshake.
bullets: PK_B protects the small session key
This is a simplified key-transport model
sections.takeaway: Protect the session key separately from the bulk ciphertext.

sections.title: Send the two protected pieces
sections.narration: Alice transmits protected key material and the authenticated ciphertext. Eve sees both without learning the message under the scheme’s assumptions. Timing, sizes, and endpoints may still remain visible.
bullets: Send protected key material and data
sections.takeaway: Ciphertext can conceal content while revealing other communication patterns.

sections.title: Bob recovers the key, then the message
sections.narration: Bob recovers K with his private key in this teaching model. He uses K to verify and decrypt the data. Verification failure requires rejection, not acceptance of untrusted plaintext.
bullets: K authenticates and decrypts the data
sections.takeaway: A hybrid receiver verifies the protected data before accepting its contents.

sections.title: Secrecy alone does not detect tampering
sections.narration: Confidentiality conceals content; integrity detects unauthorized modifications. Encryption alone is not automatically tamper-proof. A suitable authenticated scheme deliberately supplies both properties for its protected data.
sections.takeaway: Encryption and integrity are related but distinct security goals.

sections.title: An authentication tag checks the package
sections.narration: The receiver verifies the authentication tag using the key and protected inputs. Changed data should fail verification. A keyed authenticator differs from a checksum an attacker can recompute.
bullets: A checksum is not a keyed authenticator
sections.takeaway: Authenticated encryption detects invalid protected packages.

sections.title: Do not reuse nonces carelessly
sections.narration: Many schemes require a unique nonce for each use of a key. Repeating that pair can compromise protection. A nonce is not another secret key; follow the chosen scheme’s rules.
bullets: A nonce is separate from the key
sections.takeaway: Correct nonce handling is essential to secure authenticated encryption.

sections.title: A substituted public key changes everything
sections.narration: Eve replaces Bob’s public key with her own. Alice’s encryption can work perfectly yet protect the message for Eve. Authenticated key distribution prevents this identity substitution.
sections.takeaway: A public key is useful only with an appropriate trust decision.

sections.title: Confidentiality is not a sender’s signature
sections.narration: Anyone possessing Bob’s public encryption key can encrypt for him. Successful decryption alone does not authenticate Alice. Digital signatures provide a separate capability through appropriate signing and verification schemes.
bullets: Encrypting for Bob does not identify Alice
sections.takeaway: Recipient confidentiality does not automatically authenticate the sender.

sections.title: How this differs from modern TLS
sections.narration: TLS 1.3 commonly authenticates ephemeral key exchange and derives traffic keys, then uses authenticated encryption. It removed static RSA key transport, so our wrapped-key model is only an analogy.
sections.takeaway: Use the hybrid idea to understand protocols without confusing their mechanisms.

sections.title: Use established cryptographic protocols
sections.narration: Secure applications use established protocols and maintained libraries, with correct identity validation and randomness. Attractive diagrams cannot prove security; implementation, key management, and protocol assumptions must all hold.
bullets: A visual analogy is not a security proof
sections.takeaway: A sound implementation must preserve the whole protocol’s security assumptions.

sections.title: Solve the secrecy puzzle
sections.narration: Symmetric protection handles data, public-key techniques help establish suitable key material, and authentication binds the intended identities and package contents. Secure communication requires these responsibilities to fit together.
bullets: Combine key setup and data protection
sections.takeaway: Secure communication combines confidentiality, integrity, and sound key handling.
